extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in the author Forrest/Asa Carter and related literary/ethical controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style biographical article about Asa Earl Carter (who wrote as Forrest Carter), covering his life, political activities, literary works, and controversies about his identity and the reception of his books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship identity and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents that 'Forrest Carter' was a pseudonym for Asa Earl Carter, a former Klansman and segregationist; his concealment of this past and reinvention (including claiming Cherokee ancestry) are central facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider whether an author has accurately disclosed identity and past affiliations. Examples: 1976 New York Times revealed Forrest Carter was Asa Carter; the author's widow later confirmed they were the same person. The page shows how undisclosed identity can later alter reception and classification of a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of claimed ethnicity / cultural authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Carter claimed distant Cherokee ancestry and presented himself as a 'Cherokee' storyteller; members of the Cherokee nation and scholars disputed these claims and said Cherokee words/customs in The Education of Little Tree are inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should check community corroboration of ancestry claims and the factual accuracy of cultural elements. Anti-patterns include self-identification without community recognition and use of inaccurate or fabricated cultural terms. The page cites Cherokee nation disputes and scholarly criticism of inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct genre labeling and truthfulness of memoir claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The Education of Little Tree was marketed and subtitled as 'A True Story' (a memoir) but was later reclassified as fiction when the author's background came to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether publishers/authors correctly label works (memoir vs fiction). The page gives the publisher response: University of New Mexico Press removed the 'True Story' subtitle and added a fiction classification after revelations about Carter's identity. Mislabeling is a substantive editorial/ethical failure to be noted in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and sensitivity of cultural representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars and members of the Cherokee nation criticized the novel for stereotypical portrayals and romanticized 'Noble Savage' tropes; so-called 'Cherokee' words and customs were called inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should address representation accuracy and stereotyping. The page notes explicit community and scholarly objections to the portrayal of Native Americans, which should weigh against uncritical praise or inclusion on culturally sensitive reading lists without contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality (plot complexity and imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book has been criticized on literary grounds — described as having a 'simplistic plot' and relying on stereotypical imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary evaluations should consider narrative complexity, character development, and use of imagery. The page quotes Loriene Roy (ALA) noting a simplistic plot and stereotypical imagery; such literary criticisms are part of assessing the work's merits aside from ethical/identity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical reception — separating art from artist
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's history as a Klansman and segregationist affected reception: some readers and endorsers retracted support (e.g., Oprah removed the book from her recommended list), while others argued the book's message could be appreciated despite the author's past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation frameworks should include ethical considerations about endorsing or promoting works when authors have objectionable histories. The page provides examples of differing responses (removal of endorsements, defenders who separate the work from the author) that evaluators can weigh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/editorial responsibility and marketing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and editors played a role in presenting Carter as a Cherokee 'storyteller' and marketing Little Tree as a true memoir; later actions included changing covers and classifications after controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether publishers fact-checked author claims and marketed works responsibly. The page includes examples: Delacorte's original author biography and University of New Mexico Press's later corrective action; it also cites an editor defending Carter, illustrating editorial positions evaluators should consider.
